# Phaser

A `Phaser` coordinates participants across multiple phases of execution. Here,
three workers rendezvous after each of two stages: without a barrier, a faster
worker could begin the second stage before another finishes the first.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- explain how registered arrivals coordinate successive stages;
- identify the phase-advance memory-consistency guarantee; and
- describe deregistration and the consequences of a missing participant.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 8](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java8) JDK
or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in the terminal running
this example.

## The program to inspect

The constructor registers three parties before the workers start. Each worker
performs two stages of simulated work and calls `arriveAndAwaitAdvance()` after
each one. The call records its arrival and waits for the other registered
parties; the last arrival advances the phaser. The program’s “phase 1” and
“phase 2” labels describe work stages; the phaser’s initial phase number is 0.

Each worker deregisters in `finally`. In a normal run, the default `onAdvance`
terminates the phaser when the last party deregisters. The main thread joins the
workers; the phaser itself does not manage their lifecycle.

```java
final int numberOfThreads = 3;

/* Create a Phaser with a number of registered party (the number of threads working with this phaser) */
final Phaser phaser = new Phaser(numberOfThreads);

/* Create and start the worker threads */
final List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(numberOfThreads);
for (int i = 1; i <= numberOfThreads; i++) {
    final int taskId = i;
    final Runnable task = () -> {
        try {
            /* Phase 1: Simulate work */
            log("Task " + taskId + " is working on phase 1...");
            sleepForAFewSeconds();
            log("Task " + taskId + " completed phase 1.");
            phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance(); /* Indicate completion of phase 1 */

            /* Phase 2: Simulate work */
            log("Task " + taskId + " is working on phase 2...");
            sleepForAFewSeconds();
            log("Task " + taskId + " completed phase 2.");
            phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance(); /* Indicate completion of phase 2 */
        } finally {
            phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); /* Deregister this thread */
        }
    };

    final Thread thread = new Thread(task, "Thread-" + i);
    threads.add(thread);
    thread.start();
}
```

In a normal run, every `Task <id> completed phase 1.` message appears before any
worker starts phase 2. Faster workers wait for the slowest arrival, so a barrier
is useful when the next stage needs every worker’s result, but can hold up
independent tasks unnecessarily. Worker and log ordering otherwise vary.

Registration tracks counts, not worker identities or successful work. If a
registered party never arrives or deregisters, the others can wait indefinitely;
`arriveAndAwaitAdvance()` does not provide an interruptible or timed wait. Here,
an exception during simulated work causes deregistration, which can let the
remaining workers advance without that work having completed. An interruption
during sleep restores interrupt status and throws; it is not a failure protocol
for the other workers.

A `Phaser` is reusable and can register and deregister parties dynamically,
unlike the one-shot `CountDownLatch`. This example registers a fixed group and
demonstrates deregistration, not participants joining while work is underway.

## Relation to the Java Memory Model (JMM)

The JMM supplies the rules for visibility and ordering of shared state. The
`java.util.concurrent` memory-consistency contract states that actions before a
phaser wait happen-before the phase-advance action, which happens-before actions
after a successful return from the corresponding wait in other threads. This
applies to the `arriveAndAwaitAdvance()` waits here. The example exchanges no
shared results, so its output does not demonstrate that visibility guarantee.

The phaser does not make concurrent updates within a stage atomic or provide
mutual exclusion. Sleep simulates work; neither sleep nor log timing establishes
the happens-before relationship.

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from the `examples/phaser` directory. Choose one of the
following ways to run the example. In a normal run, compare the phase 1
completion messages with the phase 2 start messages; individual worker order and
timing vary.

1. Run the example using the
   [Maven `exec` plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/).

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

   This will run the example and print the following.


   (*Optional*) List the created JAR file.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   ```
   ./target/libs
   └── phaser-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   Run the application.

   ```shell
   java \
     -classpath './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main
   ```
